title: Washington misreads middle power cooperation
gist: US Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby's dismissal of a collective middle powers strategy conflates hedging with balancing: allies including India, Japan, Australia and Vietnam still treat US presence as indispensable while networking with each other because access to the American defence industrial base has been declared a privilege rather than a right, which itself supplies the rationale for diversification into critical minerals, supply chains and defence-industrial partnerships.

insights.claim: Elbridge Colby, the US Under Secretary of War for Policy, publicly argued that middle powers lack a coherent basis for alignment, remain fundamentally dependent on the United States, and would waste valuable time and political capital pursuing an alternative strategy.
insights.speaker: Biyon Sony Joseph
insights.so_what: The most senior US policy official on alliances is signalling hostility to allied minilateralism — a headwind for non-US-centric defence procurement blocs.
insights.locator: Elbridge Colby's recent dismissal of a collective

insights.claim: No coalition of middle powers can currently replicate American military capabilities or replace the United States as principal security provider in either Europe or the Indo-Pacific, and India, Japan, Australia and Vietnam continue to regard an American strategic presence as indispensable despite concerns about Washington's unpredictability.
insights.speaker: Biyon Sony Joseph
insights.so_what: US security primacy is not being displaced — reject narratives of an emerging post-American security order in Asia.
insights.locator: Colby is right on several counts

insights.claim: There is no credible substitute for much of the United States' defence technology and industrial base, even though recent operations against Iran exposed the challenges of sustaining military commitments across multiple theatres.
insights.speaker: Biyon Sony Joseph
insights.so_what: US multi-theatre sustainment strain is the concrete gap driving allied stockpiling and second-source defence procurement.
insights.locator: Nor is there a credible substitute

insights.claim: Colby's intervention has done more to elevate the middle power debate than diminish it, since a strategy dismissed as irrelevant rarely warrants such sustained public attention from one of Washington's most senior defence officials.
insights.speaker: Biyon Sony Joseph
insights.so_what: Official pushback is itself evidence that allied networking is materially consequential rather than rhetorical.

insights.claim: The central analytical error is conflating hedging with balancing: balancing seeks to counter a dominant power, while hedging seeks to reduce vulnerability by expanding strategic options while preserving existing partnerships — and most contemporary middle power initiatives are hedging.
insights.speaker: Biyon Sony Joseph
insights.so_what: A cleaner lens for reading allied behaviour: expect parallel deepening of both US ties and intra-ally ties rather than a choice between them.
insights.quote: Balancing seeks to counter a dominant power. Hedging seeks to reduce vulnerability by expanding strategic options while preserving existing partnerships.
insights.locator: Colby's central mistake is to conflate hedging with balancing

insights.claim: Strategic uncertainty encourages diversification, not divorce: demand for American engagement remains strong at the same time as middle power cooperation deepens, because countries value the United States but can no longer assume American engagement will be predictable, unconditional or sufficient.
insights.speaker: Biyon Sony Joseph
insights.so_what: Resolves the apparent paradox — allied defence budgets should grow in both US-sourced and non-US-sourced directions simultaneously.
insights.quote: Strategic uncertainty encourages diversification, not divorce.
insights.locator: This distinction explains an apparent paradox

insights.claim: Colby's assertion that access to the American defence industrial base is a privilege, not a right, was intended to reinforce US primacy but instead supplies a compelling rationale for allies to cultivate additional defence partnerships, invest in domestic capabilities and broaden their strategic options.
insights.speaker: Biyon Sony Joseph
insights.so_what: Conditional US access is the direct trigger for allied indigenous defence-industrial investment — bullish for local primes in Japan, India, Australia and Korea.
insights.locator: Ironically, Colby's own language illustrates this logic

insights.claim: There is an internal tension in urging allies to spend more on defence while expecting greater capability not to translate into greater strategic agency, since realism holds that material capabilities shape state behaviour — burden-sharing and strategic agency are two sides of the same process.
insights.speaker: Biyon Sony Joseph
insights.so_what: US burden-shifting will mechanically produce more independent allied procurement and foreign policy — the opposite of what Washington intends.
insights.locator: There is also a tension in Colby's argument

themes.theme: Functional convergence as the basis for cooperation

insights.claim: Middle power cooperation does not depend on shared identity or common ideology but on functional convergence across overlapping interests in maritime security, resilient supply chains, critical minerals, emerging technologies, defence industrial cooperation and preserving an open rules-based regional order.
insights.speaker: Biyon Sony Joseph
insights.so_what: Names the six investable domains where minilateral agreements and joint funding will concentrate — critical minerals and defence industry most directly.
insights.locator: But coalition-building has long been a defining characteristic

insights.claim: Coalition-building has long been a defining characteristic of middle powers precisely because no single one possesses the capabilities to shape regional outcomes alone.
insights.speaker: Biyon Sony Joseph
insights.so_what: Structural, not situational, driver — allied networking will persist regardless of who is in the White House.
insights.locator: Colby is equally dismissive of the basis for cooperation

insights.claim: Indo-Pacific minilateralism has been unfolding for several years — the Quad, intensifying ties among India, France, Australia, Japan, the Philippines and Indonesia, and an expanding web of minilateral partnerships — predating the transatlantic interest revived by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's remarks.
insights.speaker: Biyon Sony Joseph
insights.so_what: The specific bilateral pairings to monitor for defence-industrial and technology agreements outside the US hub-and-spoke system.
insights.locator: Nor should this debate be viewed solely through a transatlantic lens

insights.claim: Recent signals from Washington emphasising burden-sharing and evolving expectations of allies' regional responsibilities have reinforced allied incentives to network with one another.
insights.speaker: Biyon Sony Joseph
insights.so_what: US policy is the accelerant of the very allied autonomy it seeks to discourage — expect the trend to compound.

insights.claim: Middle power networks are less a vote of no confidence in American leadership than an adaptation to strategic uncertainty, and the United States should understand what drives them rather than discourage them.
insights.speaker: Biyon Sony Joseph
insights.so_what: The author's policy bottom line — a US that accepts allied agency gets more capability from partners; one that resists gets friction without preventing it.
